sentences.n: Pan doethant 'when they came': here with the ending -ant, though the next sentence has Pann doethont with -ont (and pann with nn); both endings are good third-person plural preterites, and Evans prints the two as they stand, kept as printed. wynt a welynt 'they saw', third-person plural imperfect of gwelet, soft after a. yn emmyl 'beside, at the edge of' (ymyl). yskynuaen 'mounting-block', the stone of her penance: yskyn 'mount' + maen 'stone', softened in the compound.

sentences.t: Pann doethont yn ogyuuch a hi, “A unbenn,” heb hi, “nac ewch bellach hynny.
sentences.l: When they-came level with her, “O chieftain,” said she, “go-not further than-that.
sentences.i: When they came level with her, she said, “Chieftain, go no further than this.
sentences.n: Pann doethont: see the last note; the spelling of pann and of the ending differs from the line before, kept as printed. yn ogyuuch a hi 'level with her' ← gogyuuch 'equally high', soft after yn. A unbenn 'O chieftain': she addresses the leader in the singular, but the verb is plural, speaking to them all. nac ewch 'do not go': nac with ewch, the second-person plural imperative of mynet. bellach ← pellach 'further', softened as an adverb; hynny 'than that'.

sentences.t: Mi a dygaf pob un o honawch hyt y llys.
sentences.l: I it-is-that will-carry every one of-you to the court.
sentences.i: I will carry each one of you to the court.
sentences.n: Mi a dygaf 'I will carry': dygaf is the first-person singular present of dwyn 'carry, bring', with future sense; the softening of d after a (dd) is not shown in this spelling. pob un 'each one'. o honawch 'of you' is o conjugated, second person plural. hyt 'as far as'. This is the penance laid on her: to offer to carry guests to the court on her back.

sentences.t: A hynny yw uym penyt am lad o honaf uu hun uy mab, a'e diuetha.”
sentences.l: And that is my penance for killing by me my-self my son, and his destroying.”
sentences.i: That is my penance for having killed my own son and done away with him.”
sentences.n: uym penyt 'my penance': uy (fy) 'my' brings the nasal mutation, and before p the scribe writes the nasal as m on the possessive and leaves penyt unchanged (for fy mhenyt). am lad 'for killing' ← llad, soft after am. o honaf 'by me': o marks the doer of a verbal noun, here conjugated, first person. uu hun 'myself' is written uu for uy (the Red Book has vy hun). uy mab 'my son' (m unchanged). a'e diuetha 'and destroying him': 'e 'him' as object.

sentences.t: “A wreicda,” heb y Teirnon, “ny thebygaf i y un o hyn uynet ar dy geuyn di.”
sentences.l: “O noblewoman,” said Teirnon, “I-do-not-think, I, for one of these to-go on your back, you.”
sentences.i: “Noblewoman,” said Teirnon, “I do not think one of these will go on your back.”
sentences.n: A wreicda 'O noblewoman' ← gwreicda, soft after the vocative A. ny thebygaf 'I do not think' ← tebygaf, first-person singular present of tebygu 'suppose', spirant after ny. y un o hyn uynet 'for one of these to go': y 'for' + the subject + the verbal noun, which is softened after its subject (mynet → uynet), as in modern i mi fynd. hyn 'these'. ar dy geuyn 'on your back' ← keuyn, soft after dy; di is the affixed 'you'.

sentences.t: “Aet a'y mynho,” heb y mab, “nyt af i.”
sentences.l: “Let-him-go who may-wish-it,” said the boy, “I-will-not-go, I.”
sentences.i: “Let him go who will,” said the boy; “I will not.”
sentences.n: Aet 'let him go' is the third-person singular imperative of mynet. a'y mynho 'who may wish it': the relative a with the infixed 'y 'it', and mynho, the present subjunctive of mynnu 'wish'. nyt af i 'I will not go', as Teirnon said above. The boy speaks for the first time.

sentences.t: “Dioer, eneit,” heb Teirnon, “nyt awn ninheu.”
sentences.l: “Assuredly, soul,” said Teirnon, “we-will-not-go we-for-our-part.”
sentences.i: “Indeed, friend,” said Teirnon, “neither shall we.”
sentences.n: Dioer 'assuredly', the oath (worn down from Duw a wyr 'God knows'). eneit 'soul', the friendly form of address, here to the child. nyt awn 'we will not go', first-person plural present of mynet. ninheu 'we for our part', the conjunctive pronoun, carries the 'neither'. heb Teirnon: here without the article.

sentences.t: Y llys a gyrchyssant.
sentences.l: The court they-made-for.
sentences.i: They made for the court.
sentences.n: The object put first, then a and the verb: gyrchyssant ← kyrchyssant, third-person plural preterite in -yssant of kyrchu 'make for', soft after a.

sentences.t: A diruawr llywenyd a uu yn y herbyn.
sentences.l: And huge joy that-was against-them.
sentences.i: And there was great rejoicing to meet them.
sentences.n: diruawr 'huge' (the intensive dir- + mawr, softened in the compound). llywenyd 'joy, gladness'. a uu ← bu, preterite of bot, soft after a. yn y herbyn 'against them' = to meet them: y 'their' puts h before a vowel (erbyn → herbyn).

sentences.t: Ac yn dechreu treulaw y wled yd oedit yn y llys.
sentences.l: And beginning to-spend the feast it-was-being in the court.
sentences.i: And at the court the feast was just beginning.
sentences.n: yd oedit 'one was', the impersonal imperfect of bot (-it): 'people were (at it)'. yn dechreu treulaw 'beginning to spend': two verbal nouns, the second the object of the first. y wled ← gwled 'feast', soft after the article (feminine). The adverbial phrase comes first, so the verb takes yd. The Red Book has gwled without the article.

sentences.t: Ynteu Pwyll a oed yn dyuot o gylchaw Dyuet.
sentences.l: He-for-his-part Pwyll it-was-that was coming from going-round Dyfed.
sentences.i: Pwyll himself was just coming back from his circuit of Dyfed.
sentences.n: Ynteu Pwyll 'he for his part, Pwyll' marks a change of subject. a oed yn dyuot 'was coming'. o gylchaw 'from going round' ← kylchaw, soft after o: the lord's circuit of his land, when he and his men were lodged and fed by the country.

sentences.t: Y'r yneuad yd aethont, ac y ymolchi.
sentences.l: To the hall they-went, and to wash.
sentences.i: They went into the hall and washed.
sentences.n: Y'r yneuad 'to the hall': yneuad is neuad with a prosthetic y. The phrase stands first, so the verb takes yd before a vowel: yd aethont 'they went', third-person plural preterite of mynet. ac y ymolchi 'and to wash': ymolchi 'wash oneself', reflexive ym-.

sentences.t: A llawen uu Pwyll wrth Teirnon, ac y eisted yd aethont.
sentences.l: And glad was Pwyll towards Teirnon, and to sit they-went.
sentences.i: And Pwyll made Teirnon welcome, and they went to sit down.
sentences.n: llawen uu Pwyll 'glad was Pwyll': the adjective put first, and uu ← bu, preterite of bot, softened after it. wrth 'towards'. y eisted yd aethont 'to sit they went': the purpose phrase first, then yd and the verb.

sentences.t: Sef ual yd eistedyssont, Teirnon y rwg Pwyll a Riannon, a deu gedymdeith Teirnon uch llaw Pwyll a'r mab y ryngthunt.
sentences.l: That-is how they-sat: Teirnon between Pwyll and Rhiannon, and the two companions of-Teirnon above Pwyll and the boy between-them.
sentences.i: They sat with Teirnon between Pwyll and Rhiannon, and Teirnon's two companions beyond Pwyll, with the boy between them.
sentences.n: Sef ual yd eistedyssont 'that is how they sat', the seating formula of the last part; eistedyssont is the third-person plural preterite. y rwg 'between' (rwng). deu gedymdeith ← kedymdeith 'companion', soft after deu 'two'. uch llaw 'above, on the upper side of' — the next places in honour. y ryngthunt 'between them' is y rwng conjugated, third person plural.

sentences.t: Guedy daruot bwyta, ar dechreu kyuedach, ymdidan a wnaethon.
sentences.l: After finishing eating, at the beginning of carousing, conversing they-did.
sentences.i: When they had finished eating, as the drinking began, they talked.
sentences.n: Guedy daruot bwyta 'after finishing eating': daruot 'come to an end'. ar dechreu kyuedach 'at the beginning of the carousal': kyuedach is drinking together after the meal. ymdidan a wnaethon 'conversing they did': wnaethon is the third-person plural preterite of gwneuthur without its final -t (for wnaethont), a scribal form kept as printed (the Red Book has a wnaethant).

sentences.t: Sef ymdidan a uu gan Teirnon, menegi y holl gyfranc am y gassec ac am y mab, a megys y buassei y mab ar y hardelw wy, Teirnon a'e wreic, ac y megyssynt.
sentences.l: That-is the talk that was with Teirnon: telling his whole adventure about the mare and about the boy, and how had-been the boy under their claim, Teirnon and his wife, and how they-had-reared-him.
sentences.i: Teirnon's talk was the whole story of the mare and the boy, and how the boy had been in their keeping, his and his wife's, and how they had reared him.
sentences.n: Sef ymdidan a uu gan Teirnon 'that is the talk that Teirnon had', then the verbal noun menegi 'telling'. y holl gyfranc 'his whole adventure' ← kyfranc 'encounter, adventure', soft after holl. y gassec ← cassec 'mare', soft after the article (feminine). y buassei 'had been', pluperfect of bot. ar y hardelw wy 'under their protection': arddelw 'claim, avowal'; y 'their' puts h before the vowel, and wy repeats 'they'. y megyssynt 'they had reared (him)', third-person plural pluperfect of magu, with a > e.

sentences.t: “Ac wely dy yna dy uab, Arglwydes,” heb y Teirnon.
sentences.l: “And you-see you there your son, Lady,” said Teirnon.
sentences.i: “And there, Lady, is your son,” said Teirnon.
sentences.n: wely dy 'see you!' is a presenting phrase, 'behold': it is (a) wely di 'do you see?', wely being gwely, the second-person singular present of gwelet, softened after the question particle a, which is absorbed here, with the affixed pronoun (dy for di). It is not the imperative (that is gwel). The Red Book writes weldy as one word, the later weldi. yna 'there'. dy uab ← mab, soft after dy 'your'. Arglwydes 'Lady', the feminine of arglwyd.

sentences.t: “A phwy bynnac a dywot geu arnat, cam a wnaeth.
sentences.l: “And whoever said a-lie against-you, wrong he-did.
sentences.i: “And whoever told a lie against you did wrong.
sentences.n: A phwy bynnac 'and whoever' ← pwy, spirant after a; bynnac 'ever'. a dywot 'said', third-person singular preterite of dywedut. geu 'a lie, falsehood' (modern gau), as in Rhiannon's na yrrwch geu arnaf above. arnat 'on you, against you', ar conjugated, second person singular. cam a wnaeth 'wrong he did': the object first.

sentences.t: A minheu pann gigleu y gouut a oed arnat, trwm uu gennyf, a doluryaw a wneuthum.
sentences.l: And I-for-my-part when I-heard the affliction that-was on-you, heavy it-was with-me, and grieving I-did.
sentences.i: And when I heard of the sorrow that lay upon you, it weighed on me, and I grieved.
sentences.n: minheu 'I for my part'. pann gigleu 'when I heard' ← kigleu, soft after pan: this old preterite of klywet serves for the first and the third person singular alike; here it is first. gouut 'affliction, grief'. trwm uu gennyf 'heavy it was with me' = it grieved me: uu ← bu, softened after the predicate; gennyf, gan conjugated, first person. doluryaw a wneuthum 'grieving I did': wneuthum, the first-person singular preterite of gwneuthur.

sentences.t: Ac ny thebygaf o'r yniuer hwnn oll, nit adnappo uot y mab yn uab y Pwyll,” heb y Teirnon.
sentences.l: And I-do-not-think of this company all, that-would-not-recognize the being of the boy a-son to Pwyll,” said Teirnon.
sentences.i: “And I do not think there is anyone in all this company who would not know the boy for Pwyll's son,” said Teirnon.
sentences.n: o'r yniuer hwnn oll 'of all this company'. The sentence has no subject: the Red Book has neb nyt adnappo 'anyone who would not recognize', and the White Book is read the same way, with 'anyone' understood. nit is a spelling of nyt, the negative before a relative clause. adnappo is the present subjunctive of adnabot 'recognize'. uot 'being' ← bot, softened as the object; the second witness's not is wrong. yn uab ← mab, soft after predicative yn. All kept as printed.

sentences.t: “Nyt oes neb,” heb y pawb, “ny bo diheu gantaw hynny.”
sentences.l: “There-is-not anyone,” said everyone, “that may-not-be certain with-him that.”
sentences.i: “There is no one,” said everyone, “who is not sure of it.”
sentences.n: Nyt oes neb 'there is no one'. heb y pawb 'said everyone', with the article before pawb, as before names. ny bo 'who may not be': ny before a relative clause and bo, the present subjunctive of bot. diheu 'certain'; diheu gantaw 'certain with him' = he is sure. gantaw, gan conjugated, third person masculine.

sentences.t: “Y rof i a Duw,” heb y Riannon, “oed escor uym pryder im, pei gwir hynny.”
sentences.l: “Between me and God,” said Rhiannon, “it-would-be a-delivery of my care to-me, if true that.”
sentences.i: “Between me and God,” said Rhiannon, “I would be delivered of my care, if that were true.”
sentences.n: Y rof i a Duw 'between me and God', the oath. oed 'was' here = 'would be'. escor 'deliverance, being delivered', the word for childbirth too. uym pryder 'my care, anxiety': uym (fy) with the nasal written on the possessive, pryder unchanged, as uym penyt above. im 'to me'. pei gwir hynny 'if that (were) true': pei 'if' for what is not so, with no verb. pryder is the word on which the next speaker builds the boy's name, Pryderi.

sentences.t: “Arglwydes,” heb y Pendaran Dyuet, “da yd enweist dy uab, Pryderi.
sentences.l: “Lady,” said Pendaran Dyfed, “well you-have-named your son: Pryderi.
sentences.i: “Lady,” said Pendaran Dyfed, “you have named your son well: Pryderi.
sentences.n: Pendaran Dyfed appears here for the first time, a nobleman of Dyfed; he is named again below as the boy's foster-father. da yd enweist 'well you named': da 'well' put first, so the verb takes yd before the vowel; enweist is the second-person singular preterite of enwi 'name'. dy uab ← mab, soft after dy. Pryderi echoes her pryder 'care'.

sentences.t: A goreu y gueda arnaw Pryderi uab Pwyll Penn Annwn.”
sentences.l: And best it-suits on-him: Pryderi son of-Pwyll Head of-Annwfn.”
sentences.i: And Pryderi son of Pwyll, Head of Annwfn, suits him best.”
sentences.n: goreu 'best' put first, then the particle y and gueda, the third-person singular present of gwedu (modern gweddu) 'suit, befit'; gu = gw. arnaw 'on him', ar conjugated, third person masculine. uab ← mab, softened after a personal name, as always in 'X son of Y'.

sentences.t: “Edrychwch,” heb y Riannon, “na bo goreu y gueda arnaw y enw e hun.”
sentences.l: “Look,” said Rhiannon, “whether it-may-not-be best it-suits on-him his own name.”
sentences.i: “Consider,” said Rhiannon, “whether his own name might not suit him best.”
sentences.n: Edrychwch 'look, consider' is the second-person plural imperative of edrych. na bo 'whether it be not': na with bo, the present subjunctive of bot. y enw e hun 'his own name': e hun (ehun) 'himself, his own'. She means that the name she gave is the one that fits him best.

sentences.t: “Mae yr enu?” heb y Pendaran Dyuet.
sentences.l: “Where-is the name?” said Pendaran Dyfed.
sentences.i: “What is the name?” said Pendaran Dyfed.
sentences.n: Mae 'where is?', the question word as in mae yr ebawl above; here it asks for the name the boy already has. enu is enw written with u for w (the Red Book has en6).

sentences.t: “Gwri Wallt Euryn a dodyssom ni arnaw ef.”
sentences.l: “Gwri Wallt Euryn it-is-that we-put, we, on-him, him.”
sentences.i: “Gwri Wallt Euryn is the name we gave him.”
sentences.n: No speaker is named, but the 'we' who gave the name is Teirnon's household, so Teirnon or his party answers. The name put first, then a and the verb: dodyssom 'we put', first-person plural preterite (-yssom) of dodi 'put', with ni repeating 'we'. dodi enw ar 'put a name on' = name. arnaw ef 'on him'. Wallt ← gwallt 'hair', softened in the epithet after the name; euryn 'golden'.

sentences.t: “Pryderi,” heb Pendaran Dyuet, “uyd y enw ef.”
sentences.l: “Pryderi,” said Pendaran Dyfed, “will-be his name.”
sentences.i: “Pryderi,” said Pendaran Dyfed, “shall be his name.”
sentences.n: Pryderi … uyd y enw ef 'Pryderi will be his name': the name is put first; uyd ← byd, the future of bot, softened as after the relative a, which is often left unwritten before forms of bot. heb Pendaran Dyuet: here without the article.

sentences.t: “Yawnahaf yw hynny,” heb y Pwyll, “kymryt enw y mab y wrth y geir a dywot y uam, pann gauas llawen chwedyl y wrthaw.”
sentences.l: “Most-right is that,” said Pwyll, “taking the name of the boy from the word that said his mother, when she-got glad tidings of-him.”
sentences.i: “That is most fitting,” said Pwyll, “to take the boy's name from the word his mother spoke when she had glad tidings of him.”
sentences.n: Yawnahaf 'most right', the superlative of iawn, here spelt with y for the i-glide and an extra a (the Red Book has ia6nhaf). kymryt enw y mab 'taking the boy's name' explains hynny. y wrth 'from'. a dywot y uam 'that his mother said': uam ← mam, soft after y 'his'. pann gauas 'when she got' ← cauas, preterite of kaffael, soft after pann. llawen chwedyl 'glad tidings', the adjective before its noun.

sentences.t: Ac ar hynny y trigwyt.
sentences.l: And on that it-was-stayed.
sentences.i: And on that it was settled.
sentences.n: The formula again (compare Ac ar y kynghor hwnnw y trigyssant above): y trigwyt is the impersonal preterite in -wyt of trigyaw 'stay', 'it was stayed (on that)'.

sentences.t: “Teirnon,” heb y Pwyll, “Duw a dalo yt ueithryn y mab hwn hyt yr awr hon.
sentences.l: “Teirnon,” said Pwyll, “God may-he-repay to-you rearing this boy until this hour.
sentences.i: “Teirnon,” said Pwyll, “may God repay you for rearing this boy until now.
sentences.n: Duw a dalo yt 'may God repay you', the formula. ueithryn ← meithryn 'rearing', softened as the object of dalo separated from its verb by yt. hyt yr awr hon 'until this hour' = until now; hon is the feminine 'this'.

sentences.t: A iawn yw idaw ynteu, o'r byd gwr mwyn, y dalu ytti.”
sentences.l: And right it-is for-him he-for-his-part, if he-shall-be a-gentle man, to repay to-you.”
sentences.i: And it is right that he in his turn, if he grows to be a man of gentle breeding, should repay you.”
sentences.n: iawn yw idaw 'right it is for him'. ynteu 'he for his part, in his turn'. o'r byd 'if he shall be': written as if o + the article, but the 'r is the old verbal particle ry after o 'if' (the Red Book has the same or); byd is the future of bot. gwr mwyn, as in the foster-mother's words above. y dalu 'to repay' ← talu, soft after y 'to'. ytti 'to you'.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb y Teirnon, “y wreic a'e magwys ef, nyt oes yn y byt dyn uwy y galar no hi yn y ol.
sentences.l: “Lord,” said Teirnon, “the woman who reared-him, him, there-is-not in the world a-person greater her grief than she after-him.
sentences.i: “Lord,” said Teirnon, “as for the woman who reared him, there is no one in the world whose grief will be greater than hers when he is gone.
sentences.n: y wreic a'e magwys ef 'the woman who reared him' stands first as the topic, picked up by hi later. a'e magwys: the relative a, the infixed 'e 'him', and magwys, the third-person singular preterite in -wys of magu. dyn uwy y galar 'a person greater her grief': uwy ← mwy 'more, greater', softened (the Red Book has v6y too); the cause of the softening in this descriptive phrase is not certain. galar 'grief'. no hi 'than she'. yn y ol 'after him', in his track.

sentences.t: Iawn yw idaw coffau ymi, ac y'r wreic honno, a wnaethom yrdaw ef.”
sentences.l: Right it-is for-him to-remember to-me, and to that woman, what we-did for-his-sake, him.”
sentences.i: It is right that he should keep in mind, towards me and towards that woman, what we did for him.”
sentences.n: coffau 'remember, bear in mind'. ymi 'to me', y conjugated, first person. y'r wreic honno 'to that woman'. a wnaethom 'what we did', first-person plural preterite of gwneuthur, soft after a. yrdaw 'for his sake' is yr 'for the sake of' conjugated, third person masculine (modern erddo); the log notes that Evans's r is the r-rotunda, read at high zoom.

sentences.t: “Y rof i a Duw,” heb y Pwyll, “tra parhawyf i, mi a'th kynhalyaf, a thi a'th kyuoeth, tra allwyf kynnhal y meu uy hun.
sentences.l: “Between me and God,” said Pwyll, “while I-last, I, I it-is-that will-maintain-you, both you and your realm, while I-may-be-able to-maintain my-own my-self.
sentences.i: “Between me and God,” said Pwyll, “as long as I live I will maintain you, you and your realm, so long as I can maintain my own.
sentences.n: tra parhawyf 'while I last': parhawyf, the first-person singular present subjunctive of parhau; tra usually softens (barhawyf, as the Red Book writes it), not written here. mi a'th kynhalyaf 'I will maintain you': kynhalyaf, first-person singular present of kynnhal 'support, maintain', with the infixed 'th 'you'; the softening it brings (gynhalyaf) is not written, nor in a'th kyuoeth (the Red Book has ath gynhalyaf and ath gyuoeth). a thi ← ti, spirant after a: 'both you and'. tra allwyf ← gallwyf, present subjunctive, soft after tra. y meu uy hun 'my own'.

sentences.t: Os ynteu a uyd, iawnach yw idaw dy gynnhal nogyt y mi.
sentences.l: If he-for-his-part shall-be, more-right it-is for-him to-maintain you than for me.
sentences.i: If he lives, it is more fitting that he should maintain you than I.
sentences.n: Os ynteu a uyd 'if he shall be': uyd ← byd, the future of bot, soft after a; 'be' here means 'live on, survive', a reading the sense requires but the words leave bare. iawnach 'more right', comparative of iawn. dy gynnhal ← kynnhal, soft after dy 'your' (object of the verbal noun: 'to maintain you'). nogyt 'than', a fuller form of no. y mi 'for me'.

sentences.t: Ac os kynghor gennyt ti hynny, a chan hynn o wyrda, canys megeist ti ef hyt yr awr hon, ni a'e rodwn ar uaeth at Pendaran Dyuet o hynn allan.
sentences.l: And if counsel with-you, you, that, and with these of noblemen, since you-reared, you, him until this hour, we it-is-that will-give-him to fosterage to Pendaran Dyfed from this out.
sentences.i: And if you think it good counsel, and these noblemen too, then since you have reared him until now, we will give him to Pendaran Dyfed to foster from now on.
sentences.n: os kynghor gennyt ti hynny 'if that is counsel with you' = if you approve. a chan ← can, the old form of gan 'with', spirant after a. hynn o wyrda 'these noblemen', lit. 'this of noblemen'; wyrda ← gwyrda, soft after o. megeist 'you reared', second-person singular preterite of magu, with a > e before the ending. ni a'e rodwn 'we will give him': rodwn, first-person plural present of rodi, with the infixed 'e. ar uaeth 'to fosterage' ← maeth, soft after ar. o hynn allan 'from now on'.

sentences.t: A bydwch gedymdeithon chwitheu a thatmaetheu idaw.”
sentences.l: And be-you companions, you-for-your-part, and foster-fathers to-him.”
sentences.i: And you, be companions and foster-fathers to him.”
sentences.n: bydwch 'be!' is the second-person plural imperative of bot. gedymdeithon ← kedymdeithon 'companions', softened as the complement of bydwch. chwitheu 'you for your part' (Teirnon and his men). a thatmaetheu ← tatmaetheu 'foster-fathers' (tat 'father' + maeth 'nurture'), spirant after a. idaw 'to him'.

sentences.t: “Kynghor iawn,” heb y pawb, “yw hwnnw.”
sentences.l: “Right counsel,” said everyone, “is that.”
sentences.i: “That is right counsel,” said everyone.
sentences.n: Kynghor iawn 'right counsel': the predicate first, then yw hwnnw 'is that', split by the heb-tag. heb y pawb 'said everyone', as above.

sentences.t: Ac yna y rodet y mab y Pendaran Dyuet, ac yd ymyrrwys gwyrda y wlat y gyt ac ef.
sentences.l: And then was-given the boy to Pendaran Dyfed, and joined the noblemen of the land together with him.
sentences.i: And then the boy was given to Pendaran Dyfed, and the noblemen of the land joined themselves to him.
sentences.n: y rodet 'was given', impersonal preterite of rodi. y Pendaran Dyuet 'to Pendaran Dyfed'. yd ymyrrwys 'joined, went in with' is the third-person singular preterite in -wys of ymyrru (modern ymyrryd 'interfere'); the sense here, 'commit oneself with, join', is not certain. A singular verb before a plural subject (gwyrda) is regular. y wlat ← gwlat, soft after the article. y gyt ac ef 'together with him'.

sentences.t: Ac y kychwynnwys Teirnon Toryfliant a'y gedymdeithon y ryngtaw a'y wlat ac a'e gyuoeth, gan garyat a llywenyd.
sentences.l: And set-out Teirnon Twrf Liant and his companions between-himself and his land and his realm, with love and joy.
sentences.i: And Teirnon Twrf Liant and his companions set out for his land and his realm, with love and gladness.
sentences.n: Toryfliant: Evans prints tozyfliant, run together and spelt with o, where the tale elsewhere has Twryf Uliant; kept as printed, and given in English as Teirnon Twrf Liant. y kychwynnwys 'set out', third-person singular preterite in -wys of kychwyn, singular before a compound subject. y ryngtaw a'y wlat 'between himself and his land', the idiom for setting out for a place. gedymdeithon, wlat, gyuoeth: all softened after 'y / 'e 'his'. gan garyat ← karyat 'love', soft after gan.

sentences.t: Ac nyt aeth heb gynnhic ydaw y tlysseu teccaf a'r meirych goreu a'r cwn hoffaf.
sentences.l: And he-went-not without offering to-him the jewels fairest and the horses best and the hounds dearest.
sentences.i: And he did not leave without being offered the fairest treasures and the best horses and the choicest hounds.
sentences.n: nyt aeth 'he did not go', preterite of mynet. heb gynnhic 'without offering' ← kynnhic, soft after heb. ydaw is idaw 'to him', spelt with y. tlysseu 'jewels, treasures'; teccaf 'fairest', superlative of tec. meirych 'horses' (meirch). cwn 'hounds', plural of ki. hoffaf 'most prized', superlative of hoff 'dear'.

sentences.t: Ac ny mynnwys ef dim.
sentences.l: And he-wanted-not anything.
sentences.i: And he would take nothing.
sentences.n: ny mynnwys 'he did not want': mynnwys, third-person singular preterite in -wys of mynnu 'wish, want'; the softening after ny (modern ni fynnodd) is not written. dim 'anything' (after a negative, 'nothing').

sentences.t: Yna y trigyssant wynteu ar eu kyuoeth, ac y magwyt Pryderi uab Pwyll Pen Annwn yn amgeledus, ual yd oed dylyet, yny oed delediwhaf gwass, a theccaf, a chwpplaf o pob camp da, o'r a oed yn y dyrnas.
sentences.l: Then stayed they-for-their-part on their realm, and was-reared Pryderi son of-Pwyll Head of-Annwfn carefully, as was due, until he-was the-comeliest youth, and fairest, and most-complete in every good feat, of-all that was in the kingdom.
sentences.i: Then they stayed in their own realm, and Pryderi son of Pwyll, Head of Annwfn, was reared with care, as was fitting, until he was the handsomest youth, and the fairest, and the most accomplished in every good feat, of any in the kingdom.
sentences.n: y trigyssant wynteu 'they for their part stayed' (Pwyll and Rhiannon). y magwyt 'was reared', impersonal preterite. Pen Annwn: penn with one n here. yn amgeledus 'carefully' (amgeled 'care'). ual yd oed dylyet 'as was due'. delediwhaf 'comeliest' ← telediwhaf, superlative of telediw, softened as the complement of oed. a theccaf ← teccaf, a chwpplaf ← kwpplaf 'most complete' (kwbyl), spirant after a. o pob: the softening after o (bob) is not written; the Red Book has o bop. dyrnas = teyrnas 'kingdom'.

sentences.t: Uelly y treulyssant blwydyn a blwydyned, yny doeth teruyn ar hoedyl Pwyll Penn Annwn, ac y bu uarw.
sentences.l: Thus they-spent a-year and years, until came an-end on the life of Pwyll Head of-Annwfn, and he-was dead.
sentences.i: So they spent year after year, until an end came to the life of Pwyll, Head of Annwfn, and he died.
sentences.n: Uelly 'thus' (felly; u = v). y treulyssant 'they spent', third-person plural preterite in -yssant of treulaw. blwydyn a blwydyned 'a year and years'. yny doeth 'until came', preterite of dyuot. teruyn 'end, bound'; hoedyl 'life, span of life'. y bu uarw 'he died', lit. 'he was dead': uarw ← marw, softened as the complement of bu.

sentences.t: Ac y gwledychwys ynteu Pryderi seith cantref Dyuet, yn llwydannus garedic gan y gyuoeth, a chan pawb yn y gylch.
sentences.l: And ruled he-for-his-part Pryderi the seven cantrefs of Dyfed, prosperously, beloved by his realm, and by everyone around-him.
sentences.i: And Pryderi in his turn ruled the seven cantrefs of Dyfed prosperously, beloved by his realm and by all around him.
sentences.n: y gwledychwys 'ruled', third-person singular preterite in -wys of gwledychu. seith cantref Dyuet 'the seven cantrefs of Dyfed'. yn llwydannus garedic 'prosperously (and) beloved': garedic ← karedic, softened as a second adjective after yn llwydannus, as if in one phrase. gan y gyuoeth 'by his realm' ← kyuoeth, soft after y 'his'. a chan pawb: chan ← can (old form of gan), spirant after a. yn y gylch 'around him' ← kylch, soft after y 'his'.

sentences.t: Ac yn ol hynny y kynydwys trychantref Ystrat Tywi a phedwar cantref Keredigyawn.
sentences.l: And after that he-added the three-cantrefs of Ystrad Tywi and the four cantrefs of Ceredigion.
sentences.i: And after that he gained the three cantrefs of Ystrad Tywi and the four cantrefs of Ceredigion.
sentences.n: y kynydwys 'he added, gained', third-person singular preterite in -wys of kynydu 'increase'. trychantref 'three cantrefs', tri + cantref joined, with the spirant after tri (c > ch) and the vowel weakened to y. Ystrat Tywi (Ystrad Tywi, the vale of the Tywi) and Keredigyawn (Ceredigion) lie east and north of Dyfed. a phedwar ← pedwar 'four', spirant after a.

sentences.t: Ac y gelwir y rei hynny, seith cantref Seissyllwch.
sentences.l: And are-called those, the seven cantrefs of Seisyllwch.
sentences.i: And those are called the seven cantrefs of Seisyllwch.
sentences.n: y gelwir 'are called' is the impersonal present of galw: the narrator speaks of his own day. y rei hynny 'those (ones)'. Three and four make seven, Seissyllwch (Seisyllwch), a name usually explained from the personal name Seisyll. Note that seith cantref here keeps cantref radical, while the Red Book has seith gantref.

sentences.t: Ac ar y kynnyd hwnnw y bu ef, Pryderi uab Pwyll Penn Annwn, yny doeth yn y uryt wreika.
sentences.l: And on that increase he-was, he, Pryderi son of-Pwyll Head of-Annwfn, until came into his mind wife-taking.
sentences.i: And so he continued in that increase, Pryderi son of Pwyll, Head of Annwfn, until he had a mind to take a wife.
sentences.n: ar y kynnyd hwnnw 'on that increase', put first, so the verb takes y: y bu ef 'he was'; the subject is then named in full. yny doeth 'until came'. yn y uryt 'into his mind' ← bryt 'mind, intent', soft after y 'his'. wreika ← gwreika 'take a wife' (gwreic), the subject of doeth, softened because it is separated from its verb by yn y uryt.

sentences.t: Sef gwreic a uynnawd, Kicua, uerch Wynn Gohoyw, uab Gloyw Walltlydan, uab Cassnar Wledic o dyledogyon yr ynys hon.
sentences.l: That-is the wife that he-wanted: Cigfa, daughter of-Gwyn Gohoyw, son of-Gloyw Wallt Lydan, son of-Casnar Wledig, of the nobles of this island.
sentences.i: The wife he chose was Cigfa, daughter of Gwyn Gohoyw, son of Gloyw Wallt Lydan, son of Casnar Wledig, of the nobility of this island.
sentences.n: Sef gwreic a uynnawd 'that is the wife he wanted': uynnawd ← mynnawd, third-person singular preterite in -awd of mynnu, soft after a. Kicua is Cigfa (k = c, u = f). uerch ← merch and uab ← mab, softened after a name; Wynn ← Gwynn, soft after uerch. Walltlydan 'broad-haired' (gwallt + llydan), written as one name; Wledic ← gwledic 'ruler', softened as an epithet. dyledogyon 'nobles, men of birth', plural of dylyedawc. yr ynys hon 'this island', Britain.

sentences.t: Ac yuelly y teruyna y geing hon yma o'r Mabynnogyon.
sentences.l: And thus ends this branch here of the Mabinogion.
sentences.i: And thus ends this branch of the Mabinogi.
sentences.n: The scribe's closing formula. yuelly 'thus' is uelly with a prefixed y. y teruyna 'ends', third-person singular present of teruynu. y geing ← keing 'branch' (modern cainc, also 'strain of music'), soft after the article (feminine). Mabynnogyon looks like a plural of mabinogi, but it occurs only here; the other branches end o'r Mabinogi (so the Red Book), and it is commonly taken as a scribal form (the Red Book has it too, though without yma). It gave the modern title Mabinogion. What mabinogi itself means is disputed: it is built on mab 'boy, youth', and has been explained as 'youthful deeds', 'a tale of youth' (Mabinogi Iesu Grist renders Latin infantia, Christ's childhood), 'material for an apprentice storyteller', or 'tales of the god Maponos'. None is proved. The English keeps the familiar 'Mabinogi'; l keeps the form.
